title: A book for people with lives
hookLine: written for someone living in the world, not a monastery
tomorrow: how do you add something to a life without wrecking it?

lines: A JOB, A FAMILY, A FULL CALENDAR.
cards: Can you be holy with a job, a family and a full calendar? A bishop named Francis de Sales answers with a story.

In the old days, he writes, a flower seller named Glycera could take the same handful of flowers and arrange them so many different ways that the painter Pausias, trying to paint her bouquets, gave up.
He couldn't keep up with her. Same flowers, a new arrangement every time. And de Sales, opening his book, says: that's me.
Everything about devotion has been said already. So why write one more book?

teach.b: Because of who it's for. Nearly everyone who has written about devotion, the preface says, wrote for people withdrawn from the world.
De Sales wants the others: people in towns, in households, at court, whose lives keep them out among everyone else. Same flowers; a different table.
People said it couldn't be done, that a devout life in the middle of ordinary life was impossible. He answers with nature.
The mother-of-pearl lives in the sea without taking in a drop of salt water. Fresh springs rise near certain islands, out in the ocean. A little moth flies through flames without burning its wings.
So a strong, steady soul, he says, can live in the world without taking on the world's taste. Then he names his reader. The whole Introduction to the Devout Life is written to one person, Philothea.
And here's the detail to share tonight: he explains the name himself.

teach.h: PHILOTHEA: A SOUL THAT LOVES GOD.
teach.b: It means a soul that loves God.
He built the book from notes for a real person, he says, but the name opens the door to anyone who wants devotion.
Which is the answer to the hook. Yes: holy, with the job and the family and the calendar still on the table.

how: Catholics read Francis de Sales's Introduction to the Devout Life as a guide for holiness in ordinary life; the Church honors him as a Doctor of the Church and keeps his feast on January 24.

o: an old word for a book of prayers for feast days
a saint who founded a convent in the mountains
a soul that loves God, the reader de Sales writes to

p: lives in the sea, stays sweet

s: the Introduction to the Devout Life was written for monks and nuns
de Sales wrote for people in towns, households and courts, out in the world.
de Sales explains the name Philothea himself
a soul that loves God, a name open to anyone who wants devotion.
de Sales claims to have something new to say about devotion
same old flowers, he says, arranged for a different table.

games.q: your aunt says she'll get serious about faith once she retires and has time. what would the preface say to her?
o: devotion can live inside a busy life, like the pearl in salt water.
she's right: devotion needs a quiet life away from work.
waiting is fine, as long as she reads about it in the meantime.
games.why: de Sales wrote for people whose lives keep them out among everyone else. the pearl doesn't wait to leave the sea.

practice: Look at one object that belongs to your ordinary day: your keys, a coffee mug, a backpack, a work badge. Hold it or rest your eyes on it, and let it stand for the whole crowded life it opens into.
If you pray, offer that life to God just as it is, salt water and all.

wordCard.voice: Philothea. The name Francis de Sales gives his reader: a soul that loves God, living out in the world.

orig.note: Greek-made name: de Sales explains it as a soul that loves God.

carryVoice: Your line: for people in the world. The pearl doesn't have to leave the sea. A new book, opened.
